core.text: Besides the everyday order (*pugnā!* fight!), Latin has **the future imperative (the 'you shall …' order for later or for rules: esto! memento!)**: *pugnātō!* — fight (when the time comes)! It ends in *-tō* (singular) and *-tōte* (plural) on the present stem: *amā-tō, monē-tō, scrībi-tō, audī-tō*; from *sum*: *estō, estōte*. It is the imperative (the command form) for instructions that hold from now on — laws, rules, letters saying what to do later — and a few fixed verbs: *mementō* (remember!), *scītō* (know that …). Latin name: *imperātīvus futūrī*.
English: *you shall not steal*; *be careful (from now on)*; *remember!* — orders about later or always, not about this very moment.
Present stem + -tō / -tōte (third person -tō / -ntō). It means about the same as the plain imperative, with a 'from now on / when that happens' colour.

*pugnā* (now!) and *pugnātō* (from now on / then) are both orders; Ørberg says they mean almost the same. Spot *-tō / -tōte*: that is the future one. *estō* is 'be (from now on)', *es* is 'be (right now)'.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *monitō* in *puerō monitō* (the boy having been warned, Week 2) is the perfect participle in the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form), agreeing with a noun; *monētō* with a long ē before *-tō* is 'warn!'. Check the vowel before *-tō* and whether the word agrees with a noun beside it.

The learner's notes have no page on this form. Ørberg's chapter 33 introduces it in three lines: *pugnātō, mīles! pugnātōte, mīlitēs!* — the future imperative ends in *-tō* (singular) and *-tōte* (plural) and means nearly the same as the present imperative *pugnā, pugnāte*. In the text Aemilius's letter home uses it for what his family should do after reading: *exspectātō, scrībitō, monētō, nārrātōte, scītōte*.

Allen & Greenough: the future imperative is used for orders whose carrying-out lies in the future, so it is the form of laws, wills and precepts (*rēgiō imperiō duo suntō* — let there be two with royal power), and of verbs that name a standing state: *mementō* (remember), *scītō* (know), *habētō* (consider). The third-person forms are *-tō* (singular, same as the second) and *-ntō* (plural); a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) uses *-tor* (*sequitor*). In laws the negative is *nē* + future imperative. The old-fashioned flavour is why it survives in mottoes (*estō perpetua*) and on tombstones.
